title: Tola, Jair, and God's Impatience with Israel's Misery
summary: After Abimelech, two minor judges, Tola and Jair, lead Israel for forty-five years between them. Then Israel sinks into its worst idolatry yet, serving the gods of seven nations, and the LORD hands them to the Philistines and Ammonites. When they cry out, God refuses at first, telling them to ask the gods they have chosen, but when they put away their foreign gods, he can no longer bear Israel's misery. The chapter ends with Ammon and Israel encamped for war and the leaders of Gilead searching for someone to lead them.
story: Abimelech's disastrous reign has ended, and the book pauses with two brief notices of judges who seem to have ruled quietly. Then it begins a new cycle, and this time the pattern is spelled out at greater length than anywhere since chapter 2. Two oppressors are named: the Ammonites, whose threat leads to Jephthah in chapters 11 and 12, and the Philistines, who will dominate the Samson stories in chapters 13 to 16. This chapter is the hinge between the two halves of the book's central section. It also contains the book's most revealing dialogue between Israel and God, in which the cycle itself is questioned.
historical:
Tola came from the tribe of Issachar but lived in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, a site not identified. Jair was from Gilead, the region east of the Jordan. His thirty towns, called Havvoth-jair (the tent villages of Jair), are also mentioned in Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14, where they are credited to an earlier Jair of the tribe of Manasseh. Some think this judge was a descendant who inherited or restored the name; others think the traditions refer to the same group of settlements from different times.

The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan and north of Moab, with their capital at Rabbah (modern Amman, in Jordan). They pressed on the Israelite tribes in Gilead and then crossed the Jordan to raid Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. The Philistines, on the southern coastal plain, were growing in power at the same period. The two oppressions may have overlapped in time, one from the east and one from the west. The Maonites (verse 12) are uncertain; the ancient Greek translation reads Midianites, which would fit the earlier story of Gideon. Mizpah (verse 17), meaning watchtower, was a common place name; this one was in Gilead, and it will be Jephthah's home.
cultural:
The notices about Jair's thirty sons riding thirty donkeys and holding thirty towns describe a man of wealth and standing. Riding donkeys was a mark of status for leaders and their families in this period, before horses became common for rulers; compare the song of Deborah (5:10). A large family and many towns suggest something close to a local dynasty, a pattern that will continue with the minor judges of chapter 12.

The list of gods in verse 6 covers the whole region: the Baals and Ashtoreths of Canaan, the gods of Aram (Syria) to the north, of Sidon on the Phoenician coast, of Moab and Ammon to the east (Chemosh and Milcom, named elsewhere in the Old Testament), and of the Philistines (Dagon, who appears in chapter 16). In the ancient world it was normal to honor the gods of powerful neighbors, especially when their peoples seemed to prosper. Israel's covenant demanded exclusive loyalty, which made this kind of spiritual hedging a betrayal.
literary: The chapter has two parts: the brief notices of Tola and Jair (verses 1 to 5), which follow a fixed formula of origin, years judged, death, and burial, and the long introduction to the Ammonite crisis (6 to 18). The second part expands the cycle of chapter 2 in striking ways. The list of foreign gods is seven long, as is the list of nations God has saved them from in verses 11 and 12, suggesting completeness: Israel has served every god around and been saved from every enemy around. For the first time the people confess, We have sinned, and for the first time God answers with a refusal, Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. The people repeat their confession, add action by putting away their gods, and the narrator gives one of the Old Testament's most intimate descriptions of God: he could no longer bear the misery of Israel. The chapter ends with a question hanging in the air: who will lead? Unlike earlier cycles, God doesn't raise up a deliverer; the elders go looking for one.

outline.t: Israel serves many gods and is oppressed by Ammon and the Philistines
Israel cries out, and God refuses
Israel repents, and God cannot bear their misery
The armies gather, and Gilead seeks a leader

doctrines.note: Israel moves from confession (verse 10) to surrender (Deal with us as You see fit) and action (putting away foreign gods). Repentance here is more than words; it involves removing what has taken God's place.
The seven-fold list of gods shows idolatry at its fullest: Israel served everything but the LORD. God's reply exposes the emptiness of idols, which cannot save in a time of trouble.
God's refusal in verses 13 and 14 shows that his mercy is not to be presumed on. His response in verse 16 shows that he is not unmoved by suffering. Both are true of the God of the covenant.

words.note: Chata, to sin, literally to miss the mark. For the first time in Judges, Israel explicitly confesses its sin to God (verses 10 and 15). The confession is a turning point in the book's cycle, though what follows shows how hard it was to sustain.

Bachar, to choose. God tells Israel to cry to the gods they have chosen (verse 14). The word recalls Joshua 24:15, where Joshua told Israel to choose whom they would serve. Israel's choice has now come back to face them.

Qatsar, to be short. Verse 16 says literally that God's soul became short over Israel's misery, an idiom for being unable to bear something any longer. It describes God's patience with Israel's suffering running out, not his patience with Israel.
Amal, trouble, toil, or misery. It is the word for Israel's suffering under oppression in verse 16. It often describes the hard labor and grief of human life, and here it is what moves God to act.

christ: The chapter shows a God who is moved by the suffering of his people even when they have brought it on themselves. The New Testament presents Jesus as the fullest expression of that compassion: when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). God's taunt, go and cry to the gods you have chosen, exposes the helplessness of idols, and the New Testament presents Christ as the one Savior to whom people can turn from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9-10). The chapter's closing search for a leader, one who will be head of Gilead, leaves the reader waiting for a deliverer God provides. The link is thematic rather than predictive.

hard.q: Did God change his mind, and was Israel's repentance real or only a way to get relief?
hard.a: God says he will no longer save them (verse 13) and then acts on their behalf (verse 16). Some interpreters see God's refusal as a genuine warning, withdrawn when Israel moved from words to action by putting away their gods. Others see it as a test of whether their repentance was sincere. Still others note that verse 16 doesn't say God was persuaded by their repentance but that he could not bear their misery, suggesting that God's compassion, not Israel's performance, moved him. On whether the repentance was real, readers differ as well: Israel did put away foreign gods, yet the following chapters show little lasting change. The text holds together God's judgment and his compassion, and it presents his mercy as rooted in his own character.

questions: God told Israel to cry to the gods they had chosen. If you turned to the things you rely on in a crisis, could they save you?
Israel said, deal with us as you see fit, but please deliver us today. What does honest repentance look like when you are in trouble of your own making?
Verse 16 says God could no longer bear Israel's misery. How does that picture of God compare with how you usually imagine him?
